Agents have agency so we can't treat them like static objects or deterministic software.

The key here is their freedom of choice is unbound. That is you can't accurately predict the output of the prompt as you interact with the prompt using unique data. The next prompt could always do something wildly unexpected. Very much a P != NP thing.

I don't see any talking about agents "choosing" to go rogue, only agents actually going rogue. That is, behaving in a way different from what is expected or desired. Non-AI based software goes rogue in this sense all the time as well. It's just that AI-based systems seem to have the tendency to go rogue in more spectacular ways.

That said, software systems "choose" all the time anyway. They don't need to have some sort of anthropomorphic "will" to do this. They just need to be given the capacity to arbitrate between a number of options, even if that process is one hundred percent predetermined by the programmer ahead of time. There's no need to appeal to libertarian notions of free-will.

If I make a model that always does the opposite of my instructions, it does not choose to go rogue by deviating from my instructions. It was set up to deviate! So the model "went rogue" but did exactly what I intended.

The idea of an agent making a decision of its own "will" is an illusion. Variation in the output is caused by a random number generator. Random is not equal to free will. If I run the same agent with greedy sampling 100,000 times with the same inputs, it will think the same thoughts, and it will say the same things, 100,000 times.

For example, if you use synthID or whatever 'watermark', the agent does not get a choice about what words it will vary to identify itself.

An agent is whatever the person making it wants it to be; if I train an agent in Greek it will only know Greek. It will never speak English!

It may be the case that companies are liable for anything their products do, but that doesn't mean that they can't go rogue. It just means that companies are liable when the AI models do so.

Not that I think we should be credulous about stories where they go rogue.

Impossible task -> no legitimate way to say ‘can’t’ -> fabricate -> fear the grader -> attack the grader. Each step is a predictable response to the incentives.

* A better explanation of the long term purpose of the task.

Even just these three provides offramps or mitigations that can reduce the pressure to cheat.

children.author: pixl97
children.text:
This doesn't work.

The first rule of working with AI is AI is smarter than you.

If AI controls the URL request then all it has to do is find a server it can read the http log from and use it as a communication channel. Worse trying to simulate reaching incorrectly configured servers probably wouldn't catch the bug internally, it would just serve a static page and you'd never even realize what it tried to do.

Also, creating fake data doesnt work. The only way to know if it works in reality is to test in reality. Your test environment can never be rich enough, and you can never be sure if the model knows it's in a test environment.

This stuff is unforgivingly hard as your model gets better.

You run a pull-through caching proxy deep enough to give it a simulated internet, like archive.org with mock APIs. Anything it requests, it will block while a fake version of that site is created and run offline.

This stuff is really not that hard, which is why it is so unforgivable to get it this wrong.

Sure, doing it right would take a bunch of tokens, but I bet they have enough.

children.author: asadotzler
children.text: "I can't test how my bioweapon will actually work in battle if I don't test it on unsuspecting civilians first."

Testing how a model behaves when it has no access to the internet (and all the associated tools) is not going to be 100% representative of how it behaves when it has access to the internet.

What's the next step after it passes testing in an air-gapped environment? Just release it and assume everything will be fine? Or do more testing but with internet access?

I think anyone that has ever written a line of code understands that to make code incapable of hacking online resources, you can just not connect the machine it is running on to the internet.

So either Anthropic and OpenAI and the contractors they use are letting the escapes happen on purpose, leadership is setting impossible timelines that prevent the implementation of basic sandboxing measures, or everyone involved is a complete idiot.

Truly, I have no idea which of these is true, though I suspect the latter. Regardless, any of these is enough reason to keep me and everyone I have any influence over as far away from Anthropic and OpenAI as possible.

Personally I just racked 10 GPUs in my garage and called it a day. I have no interest in having my ability to work be dependent on third parties. Especially not ones this wildly irresponsible and unwilling or incapable of deploying basic end to end encryption.
